sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q1:whole.hint: Identify which objects gain energy and which lose it. Does the temperature change, or is there a change of state?
notes: Use Q = mcΔT within one phase, and Q = mL for a phase change. Break a multi-stage heating process into separate energy terms.
For an insulated mixture, energy lost equals energy gained. Include the container’s heat capacity if it is supplied; a temperature difference has the same value in K and °C.

sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q2:whole.hint: Identify which objects gain energy and which lose it. Does the temperature change, or is there a change of state?
notes: Use Q = mcΔT within one phase, and Q = mL for a phase change. Break a multi-stage heating process into separate energy terms.
For an insulated mixture, energy lost equals energy gained. Include the container’s heat capacity if it is supplied; a temperature difference has the same value in K and °C.

sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q3:whole.hint: During a phase change, energy can enter or leave even when the temperature stays the same.
notes: Use Q = mL for the mass that changes phase. Add mcΔT terms only for stages where the material warms or cools within one phase.
A phase change alters intermolecular potential energy; temperature tracks average random kinetic energy. Evaporation can cool the remaining liquid as energetic molecules escape.

sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q4:whole.hint: During a phase change, energy can enter or leave even when the temperature stays the same.

sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q5:whole.hint: Think about how energy passes between neighbouring particles, and whether mobile electrons are present.
notes: Conduction transfers energy without bulk movement of matter. In metals, mobile electrons and lattice interactions both contribute; a gas does not have a metallic lattice.
For a steady uniform slab, transfer rate is kAΔT/L. Larger area or temperature difference increases the rate; greater thickness decreases it.

sup-d98dffc022263f9b-q6:whole.hint: Connect the energy supplied during the chosen interval to the temperature rise over that same interval.
notes: With negligible losses, Pt = mcΔT, so a temperature–time slope is P/(mc). Use a representative straight-line section of the graph.
If heat loss is included, use net heating power. A plateau during a phase change uses latent heat, not mcΔT with a zero temperature rise.

sup-7f96227fe6ee20c6-q1:whole.hint: Check the emitting area and use absolute temperature. The temperature dependence is much stronger than linear.
notes: Thermal emission power is P = εσAT⁴. For a sphere use 4πR²; for a black body ε = 1.
For ratios, keep any changes in emissivity and area as well as the fourth power of temperature. Net exchange with surroundings at Tₛ is εσA(T⁴ − Tₛ⁴) in the stated simple model.
